discovery: Theoretical prediction and modelling of kilonovae, establishing neutron-star mergers as a site of r-process nucleosynthesis
motivation: Where the elements heavier than iron are made was one of the great open questions of physics. Metzger and collaborators (2010) predicted that radioactive decay of freshly synthesised r-process nuclei in neutron-star merger ejecta powers a distinctive transient, the kilonova, and quantified its luminosity and timescale from nuclear heating rates. Kasen and Tanaka showed through atomic-physics opacity calculations that lanthanide-rich ejecta produce a red, infrared-bright emission lasting days. When GW170817 was followed by exactly such a transient, these models allowed the observed light curves and spectra to be read as direct evidence of several percent of a solar mass of heavy r-process material. Their work turned the r-process site question into a quantitative, testable one, linking nuclear masses, decay properties and opacities measured and computed on Earth to cosmic observations, and has defined the programme of nuclear-physics facilities worldwide.
